I say that rejecting the surface meaning of these views is easy once we have proved that the soul is a substance separate from bodies. Anyone with even a little philosophy knows that the soul is a noble substance, not one of the lowly bodies such as fire, air, water, or earth, and not a relation or a combination of elements. How could earlier thinkers such as Empedocles have missed what even a beginner in the study of the soul can see? It is better to interpret their words than to reject them outright.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00739

Let us begin, with God’s help. Those who said the soul moves because it is the first mover were right. The soul is indeed a kind of movement. This does not mean it is a body. Its movement is a change in its own being, from one level to another. As I have explained, it develops from sensing to understanding. At first it becomes one with sense. Later it reaches imagination. When ideas become present to it, it becomes a separate intellect.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00740

It is absurd to say that the soul of a child or embryo is exactly the same substance as a fully developed intellect among the angels, and that only its relations or outward qualities have changed. On that view, the souls of simple-minded people and children would be identical in their nature and essence to the souls of prophets, peace be upon them. Any difference between them would come from something outside their humanity: knowledge, power, or other qualities. Then the true greatness would belong to those outside qualities, not to the human being. So when we call a prophet the noblest of human beings, it would mean that something outside his real nature is nobler than what belongs to him and his people. This is wrong.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00741

The soul of a prophet, in its complete being, is nobler than the other human souls. It has more strength, completeness, light, and depth of being. It is a soul that has reached the highest level of soul and intellect. As the saying goes, “I have a time with God in which no near angel and no sent prophet can be with me.” This does not mean that the Prophet is not human in his ordinary bodily life. The Qur'an says, “I am only a human being like you.” So the human soul has different inner stages, ways of acting, and levels of development. It is always changing from one state to another. Anyone who looks within can find new states arising in the soul from moment to moment.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00742

Those who said the first mover must move by itself were also right. The first mover means what directly brings about movement. This is either nature or the soul, when a being has a soul. As I explained earlier, the immediate cause of a body’s movement in place, size, quality, or position must be a substance whose existence is changing, even if its basic nature stays the same. By natural movement I also mean movement of the heavenly spheres, which comes from their nature—their soul—and is guided by its perception and desire. The same is true of growth in plants and animals. It is natural in one way and comes from the soul in another.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00743

In general, every movement in the body comes directly from a nature that runs through it. This nature changes in its being, as we have shown. No natural body is without it. In the heavens, animals, and plants, it is inseparable from the soul. The soul is the completion of this nature. This does not mean that nature and soul are two separate substances in one body. That would be impossible. Each natural being has one self and one form. As the source of bodily movement and change, it is nature; as the power that perceives and directs, it is soul.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00744

In the previous chapter, we proved that the soul within us is the source of sensation, movement, imagination, estimation, and thought. So the ancient thinkers were right that the first source of movement is something that moves by itself—not as a body, but in its being and identity. In a living being, the soul is the first source of movement. The movement passes through it to the muscles and limbs because it is one with the nature whose being is always changing. This nature brings about all changes, including forced and accidental movement and voluntary movement. As we have seen, all of these come back to nature and soul.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00745

They were also right to say that whatever moves by itself does not die. They meant that what takes its movement from its own nature, not from something else, does not die. It does not perish; it moves from one world to another. This is not true of bodies simply as bodies, since the source of their movement is outside their material nature. Anything whose movement comes from itself is drawn toward its own completion. What is drawn toward completion by its original nature does not die, but moves from one level of existence to a higher one.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00746

Movement that comes from the self is the movement of the soul. The ordinary movement of simple elements from place to place does not come from their own essence; it depends on their moving out of their natural place. The movements of minerals and plants also need outside conditions, such as heat to cook or ripen, cold to gather, or moisture to help them take shape. The self-movement of nature does come from within, but simple elements do not last as individual things because their opposed qualities destroy them.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00747

The souls of animals and the natures of the heavenly bodies—which are the same as their souls—have life in themselves. They are always drawn toward permanence. Their movement toward completion is part of their own nature. If these souls are intellectual, like the souls of the heavenly bodies and people complete in knowledge, they return to God in the realm of separate intellects. If they are not intellectual, but imaginative or estimative, they still pass into the world of souls, at different levels of honor or lowliness, happiness or suffering. Suffering after death does not prevent a soul from developing in its own way—through cunning, animal desire, or fierce dominance. These may be forms of completion for other kinds of soul, though they are flaws in the human soul.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00748

Those who called the soul a body meant the animal’s imagined, otherworldly form, not the natural body that moves and changes here. They meant a form in the intermediate world, with animal limbs and organs. This living image is not alive because of an added quality. Through it, the rational soul acts on this natural body and perceives particular and sensible things. Those who travel the spiritual path and have direct insight agree on this. It is the form we see in dreams: we see ourselves with limbs and organs, and we see, hear, smell, taste, touch, grasp, and walk. These are spiritual organs, not our natural ones.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00749

Those who said the soul was made from indivisible particles meant imaginal bodies, which have no matter. As we have seen, they cannot be divided even in thought, much less by cutting them in the outer world. When the mind divides an imagined body, it creates two new images; it does not split one material body.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00750

Some said the soul was round because the sphere is the simplest shape, and the heavenly bodies are round. The soul was thought to be spherical because this is the easiest form to move. Through movement, the soul’s undeveloped abilities become real. We also hold that the soul and body are joined as one. The soul can therefore be described by some bodily features, since it is the source and completion of the body. This does not mean it is matter. A body’s form and material are different ways of looking at it. In the same way, a soul’s form can be described in bodily terms. The heavenly soul’s roundness is one such case.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00751

Those who said that animals draw the soul in through breathing meant that an animal has a subtle, airy spirit, clear like the heavenly bodies. This spirit serves the soul in the natural body. The soul maintains its balance, and it is nourished by clear air. Since this spirit carries the powers of sensation and movement and is continuously given by the soul to the body, these thinkers called it “the soul.” Avicenna mentions a saying in Persian: “They call the vaporous spirit jān, and the rational soul ravān.” Those who said that the soul is not this spirit but moves it from within and enters the body with it were right. This agrees with the interpretation I have just given.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00752

Those who said the soul was fire, always in motion, did not mean the basic element fire. They meant another fire: the essential heat that changes and breaks down bodies. This is nature. Above it is the fire of the commanding soul, made up of desire and anger. This is the fire that “rises over the hearts,” as the Qur'an says. When obedience and discipline calm it, the fire becomes light and the commanding soul becomes peaceful.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00753

Those who followed perception as their path were right to say that a thing perceives another because it comes before it and gives rise to it. What we directly know is an image present to the knower. To perceive something is for it to exist for the knower. This kind of presence depends on an essential relation between them: a relation of cause and effect. But the image is made by the knower; it is not physically imprinted in the knower, as we explained in our discussions of mental existence and sight.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00754

Those who made the soul from the first source—fire, air, earth, or water—may have meant the source that acts directly on the body. Those who called it fire meant what I have already described. Air may stand for desire and love, since the soul itself is a kind of love. Mystics often call the first source love. People differ in what they love.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00755

Those who called it water meant the water of life, which gives life to every living thing. As God says, “We made every living thing from water.” The soul gives life to the body just as intellect gives life to the soul. For this reason, some ancient thinkers called universal intellect the first element and likened it to water. The “first element” may mean existence itself, which flows from God to all things in order.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00756

Those who called the soul earth may have meant that it receives knowledge and images that flow from the heaven of intellect. At the level where the soul is still only potential intellect, it is like the earth of reality. Knowledge descends to it from active intellect as rain revives the earth after it is dead. A saying in the tradition puts it this way: “Hearts live by knowledge, as the earth lives by rain from the sky.”
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00757

Those who made number the source of things, and called the soul a number, meant something like what the Pythagoreans meant. The first source is truly one and gives rise to all things, just as the number one gives rise to other numbers. But the order of first, second, third, and tenth in ordinary numbers is not part of their nature. Anything that is first can become second; anything second can become first. This is not true of God, the first source: His being first belongs to His very nature. The same is true of the first intellect, and of the souls that come after the intellects. Their order in existence cannot change. So the number-like order of intellect and soul is part of their nature. They are numbers in the true sense. Likewise, only God is truly one and first; everything else is made of parts.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00758

Those who said that everything perceives what resembles it were right. As I have repeated in this book, the one who perceives is always of the same kind as what is perceived. Touch perceives what can be touched; taste perceives flavors; sight perceives what can be seen; imagination perceives imagined forms; estimation perceives meanings; and intellect perceives ideas. Each power, by taking on the form of what it perceives, realizes an ability that was previously undeveloped. What is ready to receive a thing is of the same kind as that thing.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00759

We have also proved that the intellect becomes one with what it understands, and the sense becomes one with what it senses. This union is stronger than mere resemblance. When the soul becomes intellect, it becomes all things. Even now, it becomes one with anything it holds within itself—in other words, with the image of that thing, not the external thing itself. The soul is not made up of these outside things or their images. The more complete it becomes, the more it can gather things into one, and the simpler it becomes. The truly simple being contains all things, as we have already shown.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00760

Those who combined perception and movement into one account were right if the interpretations I gave for each are right. Those who explained the soul through life alone said it was innate heat, cold, blood, or harmony. Innate heat is a heavenly substance that comes from the soul into the body, and through it the soul carries out natural, plant-like, and animal actions. In my view, this hot substance—the animal spirit—is simple and is not made from the basic elements. As I have already explained, it serves the soul and is joined to it.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00761

Those who called the soul cold may have meant the body’s condition when it is at rest and safe from harm as long as the soul preserves its balance. Those who called it blood may have meant the carrier of the animal spirit. Blood runs through the body, and through it life reaches the organs. They may have used “soul” as a shared name for blood and spirit, or as a figure of speech. People still use “soul” to mean blood.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00762

Those who called the soul a harmony may have meant that it brings the body’s elements together in a certain balance. Or they may have meant that the soul itself is made of different qualities joined in a noble, spiritual balance. The body’s balance would then be a shadow of the soul’s balance. Everything in the lower, natural world has a likeness in the higher world, but in a nobler form.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00763

Those who said that the soul was God may have meant the mystics’ idea of losing oneself in God’s unity, not the view of Pharaohs and atheists—God is far above what they say. As for the claim that God exists in each thing differently, as nature in one, soul in another, and intellect in another, I do not endorse it, to avoid disrespect. I would say instead that the human soul is nature in one sense, sense in another, imagination in another, and intellect in another. It is the substance that understands, imagines, hears, sees, smells, tastes, touches, feeds, grows, and reproduces. Yet it is one simple, undivided substance. God made it a likeness of Himself in being and qualities, and His representative in this world and the next. Knowing the soul is a path to knowing God. This is as far as I can go in interpreting the symbols and bringing out their hidden meaning.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00764
Avicenna also raises several objections to these views. I will address them briefly.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00765

First, he says that those who relied on movement must attribute rest to the soul. If the soul’s movement causes the body to move, then when the soul stops moving, the body should stop too. If the soul remains moving while the body is still, then the movement of the soul cannot be the cause of movement and rest alike.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00766

I reply that the bodily movement caused by the soul is not the voluntary movement from place to place that comes from outside reasons and later events, whether to get something pleasant or to avoid something harmful. I mean the ongoing movement of change in the living body: feeding, growth, ripening, and the other changes that happen every moment. This is the movement of life. Death is the stillness that begins when the soul is no longer joined to the body. The soul causes the movement needed for life by its own nature. It causes voluntary movement only through outside events and causes. The two are related like writing an image of a body’s organs and cooking food in a pot, compared with digesting food in the stomach.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00767
In short, the soul causes movement that does not stop while the body is alive. It does not cause stillness while it remains a soul and the body remains a body.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00768

Avicenna’s second objection is that everything that moves must be moved by something else; nothing moves itself. I agree that every movement needs a source other than the thing that moves. But something that changes in one of the four outward ways—place, amount, quality, or position—needs something to cause that change. Something whose very being changes needs a source that gives it existence. We have already explained the difference between features of existence and features of definition, and between differences in the outside world and differences created by thought. In substantial movement, movement is part of what a thing is; a being that depends on a cause for its existence depends on a cause that gives it its very being, not on something that adds movement to it. Existence is not an added feature separate from a thing, except in thought. In either case, everything that moves needs a source other than itself, and all moving things ultimately lead to an unmoving source.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00769

Third, Avicenna says that movement must be movement through place, amount, quality, position, or some other such category. I reply that there is another kind: movement in a thing’s very being. This is substantial movement. Avicenna’s argument against it is weak, as I explained earlier.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00770
Fourth, he says that if the soul changes in its essence, then it stops being a soul as it changes. Or if it changes in some feature, then that feature cannot be the source of movement.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00771

I reply that here Avicenna mixes up a thing’s existence and its definition. Substantial movement does not mean that the thing takes on a wholly new definition at every moment. A stronger or weaker state may differ in kind from another stronger or weaker state, while both remain parts of one continuous existence. The thing has one existence through time, and one definition, though each moment is a stage of its being, moving from possibility toward reality. Animal life can change into another form of animal life; it does not have to become a heavenly body. Anything that can be stronger or weaker can develop in this way. We say the same about qualities: blackness can become stronger or weaker without ceasing to be blackness. In the same way, the soul’s development does not make it stop being a soul.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00772
Even if the soul’s being a soul is a relation to the body, it does not follow that any change in the soul would make it stop being a soul.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00773

Avicenna also says that if the soul changes in one of the outward features, then it would not move the body in the same way. I reply that the earlier thinkers only claimed that whatever moves another thing must itself move in some way. They did not say that both movements must be the same kind. In many cases, the movements caused by the soul are different from the soul’s own movement. The movements of the heavenly bodies are movements of position and depend on the soul’s movement of desire and choice, as Avicenna himself admits. So there is no problem in saying that the soul’s changes in its being or desire cause changes in the body, such as digestion or growth.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00774
Fifth, Avicenna says that the claim that a thing perceives what resembles itself is impossible. We know and perceive many things that are not the sources from which they came.
Book Five — The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00775

I reply that by what is known, I mean the image present to the one who knows it and preserved by that person. The soul is the highest source of the images present in its own powers. It can take in general ideas when it is still only potential intellect; once joined with the active intellect, it creates and preserves them. In his book The Origin and Return, Avicenna says that the potential intellect can strip an image of its material features, then create and receive an intelligible form. It also acts on what is sensed and turns it into something intelligible.
